'''''Vicia ervilia''''', called '''ervil'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''bitter vetch''', is an [[Neolithic founder crops|ancient legume crop]] of the [[Mediterranean]] region. Besides the English names, other common names include: '''{{Transliteration|fa|gavdaneh}}''' (Persian), '''{{Transliteration|ar|kersannah}}''' (Arabic), '''{{lang|es|yero}}''' (Spanish), '''{{Transliteration|grc|rovi}}''' (Greek), '''{{lang|tr|burçak}}''' (Turkish),<ref>[http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/1492/legume_animal.html L.L. Bellido, "Grain legumes for animal feed"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060831002603/http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/1492/legume_animal.html |date=2006-08-31 }} in ''Neglected  crops: 1492 from a different perspective'', J.E. Bermejo and J. Leon, editors; Plant Production and Protection Series, No. 26 (Rome: FAO), pp. 273-288</ref> and '''''karshinim''''' (Hebrew).<ref>Mishna Eduyot 1:8 https://he.wikisource.org/wiki/%D7%9E%D7%A9%D7%A0%D7%94_%D7%A2%D7%93%D7%95%D7%99%D7%95%D7%AA_%D7%90_%D7%97</ref>

== Description ==

Bitter vetch is an [[annual plant]] up to {{convert|0.6|m|ft}} tall. It is insect-pollinated, and like other [[legume]]s is able to [[Nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]]. It can tolerate a range of soil types as long as these are moist and well-drained; it does not grow in heavy shade.<ref name="PFAF">{{cite web |title=Vicia ervilia - (L.)Willd. |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Vicia+ervilia |publisher=[[Plants for a Future]] |access-date=4 March 2026 |archive-date=18 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250918030912/https://pfaf.org/USER/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Vicia%20ervilia |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Cultivation ==

The nutritional value of the grain for [[ruminant]] cattle has guaranteed the species' continued cultivation in Morocco, Spain and Turkey. The crop is easy to cultivate and harvest and can be grown on very shallow, [[Alkalinity|alkaline]] soils.{{cn|date=February 2026}}

== Distribution ==

The wild strains of bitter vetch are limited to an area that includes [[Anatolia]] and northern Iraq, with an extension south along the [[Anti-Lebanon Mountains]] of Syria and Lebanon. Traces of the earliest domesticated instances were recovered from several archeological sites in Turkey, with an uncorrected [[radiocarbon dating]] of the 7th and 6th millennia BC.<ref name=Zohary/> 

== Uses ==

The grain is an excellent sheep and cattle feed concentrate. It has been held in high esteem by farmers in the Old World since the beginning of agriculture to improve the nutritional value of bulk feeds.<ref name=Enneking/>

The grain when split resembles red [[lentil]]s. For human consumption the bitterness of the seeds needs to be removed through leaching by several changes of boiling water. Owing to this bitterness, it is unlikely that someone would accidentally confuse bitter vetch with red lentils.<ref name=Enneking>Enneking & Francis (1997) [http://members.westnet.com.au/enneking/erv_97.htm "Development of ''Vicia ervilia'' as a grain crop for Southern Australia"]</ref> According to [[Daniel Zohary|Zohary]] and Hopf, this crop is consumed only by the poorest people or in times of [[famine]].<ref name="Zohary">[[Daniel Zohary]], [[Maria Hopf]] and [[Ehud Weiss]], ''Domestication of Plants in the Old World: The Origin and Spread of Domesticated Plants in Southwest Asia, Europe, and the Mediterranean Basin'', 4th edition (Oxford: University Press, 2012), p. 116</ref> 

In ancient Rome, [[Pliny the Elder]] stated that bitter vetch (''ervum'') has medicinal value like [[vetch]] (''vicia''), citing the letters of [[Augustus]] where the [[Roman Emperor|emperor]] wrote that he regained his health from a diet of bitter vetch ([[Natural History (Pliny)|N.H.]] 18.38).

The plant is linked with the [[Talmud]]ic ''borit karshina'', a plant listed in the second century as an ingredient in the [[incense offering]]s employed in the [[Tabernacle]] and the [[Solomon's Temple|First]] and [[Second Temple|Second]] [[Temple in Jerusalem|Temples in Jerusalem]].<ref name="Frumin Maeir Eniukhina Dagan 2024 p.">{{cite journal |last=Frumin |first=Suembikya |last2=Maeir |first2=Aren M. |last3=Eniukhina |first3=Maria |last4=Dagan |first4=Amit |last5=Weiss |first5=Ehud |date=2024-02-12 |title=Plant-related Philistine ritual practices at biblical Gath |journal=Scientific Reports |publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC |volume=14 |issue=1 |page= |doi=10.1038/s41598-024-52974-9  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=10861565}}</ref>
